SK1121 A try/catch is the whole body of a try/finally

An outer try/finally whose block holds nothing but a try/catch is one try statement.

CategoryModernization
Default severityhint
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

The nested form arrives by accretion — a finally added around a statement that already handled its own errors — and it hides which handler covers what: a reader has to hold two protected regions in mind to answer a question about one. One try with its handlers and its finally side by side says the same thing in the shape the language has for it.

Example

Instead of:

try {
    try {
        Copy(source, target);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        Report(e);
    }
} finally {
    source.Dispose();
}

Write:

try {
    Copy(source, target);
} catch (IOException e) {
    Report(e);
} finally {
    source.Dispose();
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Only one of the two nestings can be merged, and issue #109's own headline example is the other one. The issue proposes try { try { … } finally { … } } catch { … }. Compiled and run, that rewrite reverses the order of two side effects: the nested form logs body → finally → catch and the merged form logs body → catch → finally. .NET's two-pass exception handling runs the inner finally while unwinding to a handler it has already located, so the finally precedes the catch; a merged finally runs after its own catch. ⚠ ReSharper's inspection describes the sound nesting and the issue transcribed it backwards — the export reads "try-catch and try-finally statements can be merged", which is catch on the inner statement and finally on the outer. That is the direction this rule ships, and it is exact: an outer finally already covers the inner catch bodies, so in both spellings the finally runs after the handler, whether the handler completes, returns or rethrows — two runs of a rethrowing handler confirm it, body → catch → finally → escaped either way. ⚠ An outer `catch` is never merged, and that is the same finding from the other side. Sibling catch clauses do not chain: where the nested form lets an exception thrown by the inner handler reach the outer clause, the merged form lets it escape — measured, body → inner → outer becomes body → inner → escaped. ⚠ The outer block must hold exactly one statement, because the outer finally covers every statement in its block and the merged form covers only the inner try's; a second statement beside the inner try would be silently moved out of the protected region. ⚠ The inner statement must have no `finally` of its own. Merging two finally blocks concatenates two statement lists into one scope, where a local declared in each collides, and where a throw from the first stops the second running at all. ⚠ The comment guard is asked over exactly the two spans the edit deletes — the outer try { and the outer block's closing } — and never over the node, because a node's trivia includes the comment written above the statement (issue #302) while this edit keeps every comment in the body and in the handlers. SK0240 owns the neighbouring question of a catch that only rethrows. Generated code is excluded.
